CausalChain: Gut microbiota converts primary bile acids into lithocholic acid (LCA) → LCA accumulates in breast tissue at physiological levels → LCA binds to the TGR5 receptor on tumor‐associated macrophages → TGR5 activation triggers cAMP/PKA signaling leading to modulation of NF-κB pathways → This signaling cascade reprograms macrophages from M2 (pro-tumor) to M1 (antitumor) phenotype → Enhanced M1 macrophage activity increases immune surveillance and tumor cell apoptosis → Elevated antitumor immunity improves response to chemotherapy
Hypothesis: Physiological levels of lithocholic acid in breast tissue activate TGR5 on tumor-associated macrophages, thereby repolarizing them from a pro-tumor M2 phenotype to an anti-tumor M1 phenotype, which in turn suppresses breast cancer progression and enhances the effectiveness of chemotherapy.
Abstract: In recent years, the interplay between bile acids and tumor microenvironment has emerged as a critical factor in cancer progression. This review highlights the dual role of bile acids and their interaction with specific receptors on cancer and immune cells. Building on these insights, we hypothesize that physiologically‐relevant concentrations of lithocholic acid, a gut microbiota‐derived secondary bile acid that accumulates in breast tissue, can selectively activate the G protein‐coupled bile acid receptor, TGR5, on tumor‐associated macrophages. This activation may lead to a shift in macrophage polarization from a pro‐tumorigenic (M2) to an antitumor (M1) phenotype. Consequently, this immune cell reprogramming could enhance the host’s ability to suppress tumor progression and improve the efficacy of chemotherapeutic interventions.
